title: Where is the centre of the dots at 2, 6, 10 and 12?
description: Four dots stand on a number line at two, six, ten and twelve. The board finds the mean and then adds the distances on each side of it to check the balance. Keeko's doubt is that the centre must be eight, a whole number, because it looks like the middle.
teaching_notes: One idea: the mean is the centre where the distances on the left add up to the distances on the right, even when it is not a whole number. Watch for students who round the mean to a nearby whole number and so lose the balance.

source: Find the mean of 2, 6, 10 and 12 and check the balance.
video_script.why: The child checks the balance of a mean that is not a whole number, and sees that the centre can sit between the marks.
video_script.substitution: Place each number as a dot on a number line and add the distances from the mean to the dots on each side.
video_script.anchor: a number line with four dots at two, six, ten and twelve
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the centre is eight. From eight the left distances add to eight but the right distances add to six, so eight does not balance and the true centre is seven and a half.
video_script.payoff_line: The mean is seven point five

final_answer.value: The mean is 7.5 and the distances on both sides add to 7
final_answer.spoken: the mean is seven point five, and the distances on both sides add to seven

hold_back: Answer: The mean is 7.5 and the distances on both sides add to 7
never_show: the final answer line before the answer beat
maths_rules: Keeko's doubt: from 8, left 6 + 2 = 8 and right 2 + 4 = 6, so 8 does not balance
video_script.design: One idea: the mean is the centre that balances the distances, even between marks. The number line stays from ground to the end of the idea part. Wrong idea: the centre is the nearby whole number eight.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the centre is eight, because eight is a neat whole number.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>From eight, the left side adds to eight and the right side adds to six. Eight does not balance the distances.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Only seven point five balances, so never round the mean to a whole number.
